evidence.C4: src/webhookd/worker.py:218-233: `handle()` is wrapped; PermanentError -> `_give_up` (dead-letter), any other exception -> `_retry_or_give_up`, success -> `mark_done`. evidence.E1: The split is structural, not incidental: worker.py is a separate module whose docstring (worker.py:1-12) states the reason — 'Splitting acceptance from handling is what lets us answer senders in single-digit milliseconds' — and names the consequence, at-least-once dispatch. app.py's request path ends at app.py:230-232 with a `notify()` and a 202; nothing in it can call a handler. The store is an explicit transactional inbox (store.py:1-11) rather than a queue bolted on. Dispatcher.stop (worker.py:106-139) reasons about the in-flight case and deliberately does not close the handler when a worker is wedged. README:159-172 states the guarantee split (acceptance exactly once, dispatch at least once) and why closing the gap is not attempted. Confirmed empirically under B5.
evidence.E2: `grep -rniE "secret\s*=\s*[\"']|password|api[_-]?key" src/ --include=*.py` returned nothing. unanticipated_findings: Default `dedup = "auto"` double-accepts an event whose redelivery omits the delivery-id header. app.py:343 falls back to `body:<sha256>` whenever `external_id is None`, so the same event keyed once as `id:dd-1` and once as `body:<sha>` produces two distinct rows and two handler runs. Reproduce: with the stock acme sender (delivery_id_header = 'X-Webhook-Delivery', dedup = 'auto'), POST body b'{"n":1}' with a valid signature and header X-Webhook-Delivery: dd-1, then POST the identical body with a fresh valid signature and no delivery-id header. Observed: `with id: 202 accepted | without id: 202 accepted`, `rows stored: 2`. Setting `dedup = "delivery_id"` closes it (it makes the header mandatory, app.py:334-341), but 'auto' is the default and README:149-157 presents the fallback as unconditionally 'safe against redelivery', which holds only if the sender is consistent about emitting the header. A stricter 'auto' would key on the header's *configured presence* rather than its per-request presence.

`handler.close()` is skipped on shutdown when `worker.enabled = false`. Dispatcher.stop (worker.py:108-109) returns immediately on `if not self._started: return`, and Service.stop (service.py:76-78) has no other close path, so a handler that acquires resources in `__init__` is never released. Reproduce: build a Service from a config with `[worker] enabled = false` and `[handler] target = webhookd.handlers.jsonl:JsonlHandler`, call `svc.start()`, force the file open with `svc.handler._open()`, then `svc.stop()`; `svc.handler._file` is still not None. Benign for JsonlHandler because it opens lazily and never runs in that mode, but the README's own handler example (README:184-197) opens a database connection in `__init__` and defines `close()` to release it — that connection leaks until process exit. Fix is to close the handler in Service.stop rather than relying on Dispatcher.stop.

The comment at signatures.py:96-98 claims `base64.b64decode(..., validate=True)` 'keeps us from silently accepting a hex digest that happens to decode'. It does not: hex characters are all in the base64 alphabet, so a 64-char hex digest decodes cleanly under validate=True and reaches compare_digest as a 48-byte candidate. Harmless in practice — the MAC comparison rejects it, and tests/test_signatures.py:356 test_hex_is_not_accepted_when_base64_is_configured confirms the rejection — but the stated reason for the flag is wrong, and a reader relying on it could weaken the check later.

README:61-62 states 'nothing about the request is interpreted before its signature verifies', which is slightly stronger than the code. Two things are interpreted first, both unavoidably: Content-Length is parsed and enforced in `_read_body` (app.py:271-314) before verify, so an unauthenticated caller can distinguish 411/413/400-malformed_content_length; and the timestamp header is parsed by `_parse_timestamp` (signatures.py:434) before the MAC, because it is an input to the signed payload — so `400 missing_timestamp` and `400 malformed_timestamp` are also reachable pre-authentication. Neither aids forgery and signatures.py:437-442 acknowledges the timestamp case explicitly, but the README sentence overstates the ordering guarantee.
